evidence_text: Atorvastatin is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of heart attack, stroke, angina, and to decrease the chance that heart surgery will be needed in people who have heart disease or who are at risk of developing heart disease.
Atorvastatin helps lower LDL cholesterol ('bad cholesterol') and triglyceride levels, and increases HDL cholesterol ('good cholesterol') levels, to improve your overall lipid profile.
Atorvastatin calcium belongs to a class of medications called HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, commonly referred to as statins.

Atorvastatin works by selectively blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the key enzyme the liver uses to produce cholesterol. By slowing this process, it reduces cholesterol production in the liver and increases the number of LDL receptors on liver cells, which helps remove more LDL (“bad”) cholesterol from the bloodstream.

As an adjunct to diet to lower LDL-C:
- Adults with primary hyperlipidemia.
- Adults and pediatric patients (10 years and older) with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH).

As an adjunct to other LDL-lowering therapies:
- For adults and pediatric patients (10 years and older) with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia.

As an adjunct to diet for additional lipid disorders in adults:
- Primary dysbetalipoproteinemia.
- Hypertriglyceridemia.
You should not take atrovastatin calcium if you have liver disease or cirrhosis.

Atorvastatin calcium can cause the breakdown of muscle tissue, which can lead to kidney failure. Call your doctor right away if you have unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness, especially if you also have fever, unusual tiredness, or dark urine.

Tell your healthcare professional if you are pregnant, or plan to become pregnant, or become pregnant. Atorvastatin may harm your unborn baby. If you become pregnant, stop taking atorvastatin and call your healthcare provider right away.

Tell your healthcare professional if you are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed. You and your healthcare provider should decide if you will take this medicine or breastfeed. You should not take atorvastatin if you breastfeed. Talk to your healthcare provider about the best way to feed your baby if you take LIPITOR.

Recommended Dosage in Adult Patients The recommended starting dosage of Lipitor is 10 mg to 20 mg once daily. The dosage range is 10 mg to 80 mg once daily. Patients who require a reduction in LDL-C greater than 45% may be started at 40 mg once daily.
Recommended Dosage in Pediatric Patients 10 Years of Age and Older with HeFH The recommended starting dosage of Lipitor is 10 mg once daily. The dosage range is 10 mg to 20 mg once daily.

Levothyroxine is a man-made form of thyroxine (T4), one of the hormones your thyroid gland normally produces. It belongs to a class of medications called hormones, and it works by replacing thyroid hormone that your body is not making enough of.

Levothyroxine is used in adults and children, including newborn babies, to:
- treat hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid - a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone). It replaces the missing hormone whether the condition was present from birth or developed later, and whether the problem starts in the thyroid gland itself or in the pituitary gland or hypothalamus; and

Levothyroxine is used in adults and children, including newborn babies, to:
- treat hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid - a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone). It replaces the missing hormone whether the condition was present from birth or developed later, and whether the problem starts in the thyroid gland itself or in the pituitary gland or hypothalamus; and
- lower the level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the blood in people being treated for a certain type of thyroid cancer, alongside surgery and radioactive iodine therapy.
Levothyroxine injection is used in adults to treat myxedema coma, a rare and life-threatening complication of a severely underactive thyroid.

Levothyroxine is not used to shrink benign (noncancerous) thyroid nodules or a nontoxic diffuse goiter in people who get enough iodine in their diet. It does not help in these situations, and taking more thyroid hormone than your body needs can cause an overactive thyroid. It is also not used to treat hypothyroidism during the recovery phase of subacute thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid gland).
Levothyroxine is not used to treat obesity or for weight loss.

Levothyroxine has a narrow therapeutic index, which means the difference between too little and too much is small. Taking too much or too little over time can affect your heart, bones, blood sugar, cholesterol, digestion, memory and concentration, fertility, and, in children, growth and development. Your doctor will start you on a suitable dose and adjust it gradually based on blood tests.

If you have an adrenal gland problem, you will need to start treatment with a steroid (glucocorticoid) medicine before you start levothyroxine. Starting levothyroxine first can trigger a sudden, serious drop in adrenal hormones known as an adrenal crisis.

Taking more levothyroxine than your body needs over a long period can weaken your bones and lead to a higher risk of fractures. This is more likely after menopause. Your doctor will aim to give you the lowest dose that controls your thyroid levels.
Oral levothyroxine should not be used to treat myxedema coma. Levothyroxine given into a vein is used instead.
You should not use levothyroxine if you have an untreated or uncontrolled adrenal gland disorder.
Oral levothyroxine is taken by mouth and is available as tablets, capsules, and an oral solution.

Take levothyroxine tablets and capsules on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast with a full glass of water. A full glass of water is important to avoid choking or gagging, because the tablet can start to break apart quickly. Take the medicine at the same time each day.

Avoid the following food products within 1 hour of taking oral levothyroxine or the medication will not be as effective: grapefruit juice, infant soy formula, soybean flour, cottonseed meal, walnuts, and high-fiber foods. Grapefruit juice can both delay absorption and reduce the amount of levothyroxine that gets into your body.

Metformin is a first-line treatment used for type 2 diabetes in adults and children 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar levels. It is also used off-label to improve symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) and other conditions. Metformin tablets should be used together with dietary changes and exercise for better results.
Metformin belongs to the drug class biguanides.

Metformin works by reducing glucose absorption from the intestines, lowering liver glucose production, and improving insulin sensitivity. Managing blood sugar levels with medications like metformin can prevent diabetes complications such as kidney damage, nerve issues, blindness, amputations, sexual dysfunction, and lower the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Metformin has a boxed warning for lactic acidosis, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood, which can cause death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA.
Vitamin B12 deficiency: Metformin can lower your vitamin B12 levels over time. Your doctor may check your blood counts every year and your B12 levels every 2 to 3 years to catch any problems early.

Low blood sugar when taken with insulin or other diabetes medicines: Taking metformin along with insulin or certain other diabetes drugs (ones that boost insulin release) raises the risk of low blood sugar. If you're on one of these combinations, your doctor may lower the dose of the other medicine.

Common side effects of metformin hydrochloride tablets include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, wind (flatulence), indigestion, and headache. These side effects occurred in 5% or more of patients in the US clinical trial of using metformin for type 2 diabetic patients. In the same study, 6% of patients discontinued metformin due to diarrhea.

You should not use metformin if you have:
- severe kidney disease, or
- metabolic acidosis or diabetic ketoacidosis (call your doctor for treatment), or
- an allergy to metformin or any of the inactive ingredients in this medicine.
Metformin immediate release tablets should not be given to a child younger than 10 years old.
This medicine should not be used for type 1 diabetes.

Talk to your healthcare provider if you are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed. Metformin can pass into your breast milk. Your healthcare provider will be able to advise you about the best way to feed your baby while you take this medicine.
Take metformin with a meal, unless your doctor tells you otherwise. Some forms of metformin are taken only once daily with the evening meal. Follow your doctor's instructions.

Immediate-release tablets:
Initial dose: 500 mg orally twice a day or 850 mg orally once a day Dose titration: Increase by 500 mg increments weekly or 850 mg every 2 weeks as tolerated. Maintenance dose: 2000 mg/day in divided doses Maximum dose: 2550 mg/day. Doses above 2,000 mg may be better tolerated given 3 times

Usual Adult Metformin Dose for Diabetes Type 2:
Immediate-release tablets:
Initial dose: 500 mg orally twice a day or 850 mg orally once a day Dose titration: Increase by 500 mg increments weekly or 850 mg every 2 weeks as tolerated. Maintenance dose: 2000 mg/day in divided doses Maximum dose: 2550 mg/day. Doses above 2,000 mg may be better tolerated given 3 times
Extended-release tablets:
Initial dose: 500 to 1000 mg orally once a day Dose titration: Increase in 500 mg increments weekly as tolerated Maximum dose: 2000 mg/day
- Do not use this medicine in patients with eGFR below 30 mL/minute/1.73 m 2
- It is not recommended to start metformin tablets in patients with eGFR between 30 to 45 mL/minute/1.73 m 2

Medicines that have a carbonic anhydrase inhibiting effect like topiramate (often used for seizures or migraines), zonisamide (used for seizures), acetazolamide (used for glaucoma, altitude sickness, and other conditions), and dichlorphenamide (used for a muscle condition called periodic paralysis) can raise the risk of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis when taken with metformin. These medicines commonly lower a substance in your blood called bicarbonate, which your body needs to keep its acid levels balanced. If you're taking metformin along with any of these medicines, your doctor may want to monitor you more closely.

Other medicines that may increase risk of lactic acidosis. Some medicines including cimetidine (used for heartburn), ranolazine (used for chest pain/angina), dolutegravir (used to treat HIV), and vandetanib (used to treat certain thyroid cancers) can all cause metformin levels to increase. They do this by blocking the same pathway your kidneys use to clear metformin out of your system. Since higher metformin levels raise the risk of lactic acidosis, your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks before prescribing any of these together with metformin.
Alcohol: Drinking alcohol, especially in large amounts or regularly, can make it harder for your body to process metformin normally and raises the risk of lactic acidosis.

Amlodipine besylate is a prescription medicine used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and to prevent certain types of angina (chest pain). It belongs to a class of medications called calcium channel blockers.
Amlodipine besylate works by relaxing and widening the blood vessels, so blood flows more easily which improves blood pressure.

Amlodipine besylate controls angina chest pain by increasing the supply of blood to the heart. If taken regularly, this medicine controls chest pain, but it does not stop chest pain once it starts. Your doctor may prescribe a different medication to take when you have chest pain.

Amlodipine is also used alone or in combination with other medicines to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) in adults and children at least 6 years old. Lowering blood pressure may lower your risk of a stroke or heart attack.

In rare cases, when you first start taking this medicine, your chest pain may get worse or you could have a heart attack. Seek emergency medical attention or call your doctor right away if you have symptoms such as: chest pain or pressure, pain spreading to your jaw or shoulder, nausea, sweating.
Drinking alcohol can further lower your blood pressure and may increase certain side effects of amlodipine.
You should not take amlodipine if you are allergic to it.
Do not breastfeed while taking amlodipine. You can stop breastfeeding or take a different medicine.

Usual Amlodipine Adult Dose for Hypertension:
Initial dose: 5 mg orally once a day Maintenance dose: 5 to 10 mg orally once a day Maximum dose: 10 mg/day Comments: Patients who are small or fragile may be started on 2.5 mg orally once a day.

Usual Geriatric Dose for Hypertension:
Initial dose: 2.5 mg orally once a day Maintenance dose: 2.5 to 10 mg orally once a day Maximum dose: 10 mg/day.

Usual Pediatric Dose for Hypertension:
6 to 17 years: -Maintenance dose: 2.5 to 5 mg orally once a day -Maximum dose: 5 mg/day Comments: Doses higher than 5 mg have not been studied in pediatric patients. The dosage should be adjusted according to patient response. In general, titration should proceed over 7 to 14 days. If clinically warranted, titration may proceed more rapidly, provided the patient is assessed frequently. Use: Alone or in combination with other antihypertensive agents to treat hypertension
Tell your doctor if you take simvastatin. You should not take more than 20 mg of simvastatin daily while taking amlodipine.
Lisinopril is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children 6 years of age and older.
Lisinopril is also used in adults to treat congestive heart failure and to improve survival after a heart attack.

Lisinopril belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors. It works by decreasing certain chemicals that tighten the blood vessels, so blood flows more smoothly and the heart can pump blood more efficiently.
Do not use lisinopril if you are pregnant. It could harm the unborn baby. Stop using this medicine and tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant.
You should not use this medicine if you have ever had angioedema. Do not take lisinopril within 36 hours before or after taking medicine that contains sacubitril (such as Entresto).
If you have diabetes, do not use lisinopril together with any medication that contains aliskiren (such as Amturnide, Tekturna, Tekamlo).
You may also need to avoid taking lisinopril with aliskiren if you have kidney disease.

You should not use lisinopril if you are allergic to it or to any other ACE (angiotensin converting enzyme) inhibitor such as captopril, fosinopril, enalapril, benazepril, moexipril, perindopril, quinapril, ramipril, or trandolapril.
Stop using this medicine and tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Lisinopril can cause injury or death to the unborn baby if you use the medicine during your second or third trimester.

Usual Adult Dose for Hypertension:
Initial dose: 10 mg orally once a day; 5 mg orally once a day Maintenance dose: 20 to 40 mg orally once a day Maximum dose: 80 mg orally once a day Comments: -The initial dose is 5 mg orally once a day in patients receiving a diuretic. -The 80 mg dose is used but does not appear to give greater effect. -If blood pressure is not controlled with lisinopril alone, a low dose of a diuretic may be added (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, 12.5 mg). After the addition of a diuretic, it may be possible to reduce the dose of lisinopril.

Usual Adult Dose for Congestive Heart Failure:
Initial dose: 2.5 to 5 mg orally once a day Maintenance dose: Dosage should be increased as tolerated Maximum dose: 40 mg orally once a day Comments: -The diuretic dose may need to be adjusted to help minimize hypovolemia, which may contribute to hypotension. The appearance of hypotension after the initial dose of lisinopril does not preclude subsequent careful dose titration with the drug.

Usual Adult Dose for Diabetic Nephropathy:
Initial dose: 10 to 20 mg orally once a day Maintenance dose: 20 to 40 mg orally once a day Dosage may be titrated upward every 3 days Comments: -Not an approved indication.

Common lisinopril side effects may include:
- headache, dizziness;
- low blood pressure, cough; or
- chest pain.
Lisinopril can harm your kidneys, especially if you also use certain medicines for infections, cancer, or osteoporosis.
Albuterol is a bronchodilator that relaxes muscles in the airways and increases air flow to the lungs.

Albuterol inhalation is used to treat or prevent bronchospasm, or narrowing of the airways in the lungs, in people with asthma or certain types of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It is also used to prevent exercise-induced bronchospasm.
Albuterol inhalation is for use in adults and children who are at least 2 years old. Always follow your doctor's directions when giving albuterol to a child.
Only use albuterol as prescribed by your physician. An overdose of albuterol can be fatal. Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
You should not use this medicine if you are allergic to albuterol. You should not use ProAir RespiClick or ProAir Digihaler if you are allergic to milk proteins.

The usual dose of albuterol inhalation is 2 inhalations every 4 to 6 hours. To prevent exercise-induced bronchospasm, use 2 inhalations 15 to 30 minutes before you exercise. The effects of albuterol inhalation should last about 4 to 6 hours.
Losartan is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children at least 6 years old.

Losartan is also used to decrease the risk of stroke in people who have high blood pressure and a heart condition called left ventricular hypertrophy (enlargement of the walls of the left side of the heart).
Losartan may not decrease the risk of stroke in African Americans who have these conditions.

Losartan is also used to treat kidney disease in people who have type 2 diabetes (condition in which the body does not use insulin normally and therefore cannot control the amount of sugar in the blood) and high blood pressure.

Losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin II receptor antagonists. It works by blocking the action of certain natural substances that tighten the blood vessels, allowing the blood to flow more smoothly and the heart to pump more efficiently.
Do not use losartan if you are pregnant, and tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. It can cause injury or death to the unborn baby.
If you have diabetes, do not use losartan together with any medication that contains aliskiren (a blood pressure medicine).
You may also need to avoid taking losartan with aliskiren if you have kidney disease.

In rare cases, this medicine can cause a condition that results in the breakdown of skeletal muscle tissue, leading to kidney failure. Call your doctor right away if you have unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness especially if you also have fever, unusual tiredness, and dark colored urine.
You should not use losartan if you are allergic to it.
You should not breastfeed while using this medicine and for 2 days after your last dose.
- Losartan is usually taken once per day.
- You may take losartan with or without food.

Usual Adult Dose for Hypertension:
Initial dose: 50 mg orally once a day Maximum dose: 100 mg orally once a day Comments: -If hypertensive patients with left ventricular hypertrophy or type 2 diabetic nephropathy patients require titration from initial dose, increase to 100 mg orally once a day. -Antihypertension is substantially present within 1 week but in some studies the maximal effect occurred in 3 to 6 weeks. Uses: -Treatment of hypertension. -To reduce the risk of stroke in patients with hypertension and left ventricular hypertrophy. -Treatment of diabetic nephropathy with an elevated serum creatinine and proteinuria (urinary albumin to creatinine ratio 300 mg/g or greater) in patients with type 2 diabetes and a history of hypertension.

Usual Pediatric Dose for Hypertension:
6 Years or Older: Initial dose: 0.7 mg/kg orally once a day (up to 50 mg total) Comments: -May be given as a tablet or suspension. If using the suspension, use an oral dosing syringe or an oral dosing cup to measure the prescribed dose. Do not use a teaspoon or tablespoon. -Doses above 1.4 mg/kg (or 100 mg) daily have not been studied in pediatric patients.
Do not use potassium supplements or salt substitutes, unless your doctor has told you to.

Tell your doctor about all your other medicines, especially:
- a diuretic or "water pill" that may increase blood potassium such as spironolactone, triamterene, amiloride;
- NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) - aspirin, ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), celecoxib, diclofenac, indomethacin, meloxicam, and others; or
- heart or blood pressure medication.
- lithium.

Metoprolol is a beta-blocker medication used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and heart failure, and to improve survival after a heart attack. It works mainly on the heart, so it is called a cardioselective beta-blocker.

Metoprolol works by blocking the effect of adrenaline and noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors in your heart. This slows your heart rate, reduces how hard your heart squeezes, and lowers your blood pressure. Because the heart is doing less work, it needs less oxygen, which is why metoprolol also helps with angina. Exactly how metoprolol works for high blood pressure, heart failure, and after a heart attack is not fully understood.
At higher blood levels, metoprolol also blocks beta-2 receptors in the airways and blood vessels, which is why it still needs care in people with breathing problems.
- Metoprolol tartrate, an immediate-release tablet usually taken once or twice a day (brand name Lopressor)
- Metoprolol succinate, an extended-release tablet or capsule taken once a day (brand names Toprol-XL and Kapspargo Sprinkle)

Angina. Metoprolol is used for long-term treatment of angina, to reduce how often attacks happen and to help you do more before chest pain starts. It is not used to stop an attack that has already begun.

Heart failure. Only the extended-release form is approved for heart failure. It is used to reduce the risk of dying from heart and blood vessel causes and to reduce hospital admissions for heart failure.

The most important warning with metoprolol is not to stop it suddenly. Stopping a beta blocker abruptly can bring on worse chest pain and, in some cases, a heart attack. If your treatment needs to stop, your prescriber will lower the dose gradually over 1 to 2 weeks and watch how you respond. This applies even if you only take metoprolol for blood pressure, because heart disease is common and is not always known about.

- Diabetes or long gaps without food. Metoprolol can hide the early warning signs of low blood sugar, such as a fast heartbeat, and can make low blood sugar more severe or last longer. The risk is higher if you are fasting, not eating regularly, or vomiting.

You should not take metoprolol if you have a very slow heart rate, heart block beyond the first degree, sick sinus syndrome without a pacemaker, cardiogenic shock, or heart failure that is not under control.
- Take fluoxetine, paroxetine, quinidine, or propafenone, which raise metoprolol levels in your blood

Condition | Starting dose | Usual range
High blood pressure | 100 mg a day, as one dose or split into two | 100 mg to 450 mg a day. Doses above 450 mg a day have not been studied.

Metoprolol succinate (extended-release tablets and capsules) dosage for adults:
Condition | Starting dose | Usual range
High blood pressure | 25 mg to 100 mg once a day | Adjust weekly or less often. Doses above 400 mg a day have not been studied.
Rosuvastatin (Crestor) is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events such as heart attack and stroke.

Rosuvastatin belongs to a class of medicines called statins. It works by blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol. With cholesterol synthesis reduced, the liver increases its LDL receptors and clears more LDL, or "bad" cholesterol, from the blood. LDL and total cholesterol levels fall, with the maximum reduction usually reached by four weeks.

Rosuvastatin comes as a tablet. It was first approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on August 12, 2003, under the brand name Crestor. Many generic versions of rosuvastatin tablets have since been approved.

Rosuvastatin is used:
- to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular (CV) events, such as death from cardiovascular disease, heart attack, stroke, or the need for procedures to improve blood flow to the heart called arterial revascularization, in adults at increased risk for these events.

Rosuvastatin is used:
- to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular (CV) events, such as death from cardiovascular disease, heart attack, stroke, or the need for procedures to improve blood flow to the heart called arterial revascularization, in adults at increased risk for these events.
- along with diet and exercise to lower the level of low-density lipoprotein (LDL-C) cholesterol or "bad" cholesterol: in adults with primary hypercholesterolemia. and slow the buildup of fatty deposits (plaque) in the walls of blood vessels in adults. in adults and children 8 years of age and older with high blood cholesterol due to heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) (an inherited condition that causes high levels of LDL-C). in adults and children 7 years of age and older with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HoFH) (an inherited condition that causes high levels of LDL-C).
- along with diet for the treatment of adults with: primary dysbetalipoproteinemia (an inherited condition that causes high levels of cholesterol and fat). hypertriglyceridemia.
The most common side effects may include headache, nausea, muscle aches and pains, weakness, and constipation.

Rosuvastatin may cause serious side effects, including:
- Muscle pain, tenderness and weakness (myopathy). Muscle problems, including muscle breakdown, can be serious in some people and rarely cause kidney damage that can lead to death. Tell your doctor right away if: you have unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness, especially if you have a fever or feel more tired than usual, while you take this medicine. you have muscle problems that do not go away even after your doctor has told you to stop taking this medicine. Your doctor may do further tests to diagnose the cause of your muscle problems. Your chances of getting muscle problems are higher if you: are taking certain other medicines while you take rosuvastatin are 65 years of age or older are of Asian descent have thyroid problems (hypothyroidism) that are not controlled have kidney problems are taking higher doses of this medicine
- Liver problems. Your doctor may do blood tests to check your liver before you start taking this medicine and if you have symptoms of liver problems while you are taking it. Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following symptoms of liver problems: feel unusually tired or weak loss of appetite upper belly pain dark urine yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes
- Protein and blood in the urine. Rosuvastatin may cause you to have protein and blood in your urine. If you develop protein or blood in your urine, your doctor may decrease your dose.
- Increase in blood sugar (glucose) levels. Rosuvastatin may cause an increase in your blood sugar levels.

Do not take rosuvastatin if you:
- are allergic to rosuvastatin or any of the ingredients in your rosuvastatin tablets. See below for a complete list of ingredients.
- have liver problems.
- Dose range: 5 mg to 40 mg once daily. The dose depends on the reason you are taking it, your LDL cholesterol level, and your individual risk of cardiovascular events.
- People of Asian descent: the recommended starting dose is 5 mg once daily.
- Severe kidney impairment (not on hemodialysis): the recommended starting dose is 5 mg once daily, and the dose should not exceed 10 mg once daily.
- Children with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia: 20 mg once daily for those 7 years of age and older.

Taking rosuvastatin with certain medicines may increase the risk of muscle problems. Especially tell your doctor if you take:
- cyclosporine (a medicine for your immune system)
- teriflunomide (a medicine used to treat relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis)
- enasidenib (a medicine used to treat acute myeloid leukemia)
- capmatinib (a medicine for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer)
- fostamatinib (a medicine used to treat low platelet counts)
- febuxostat (a medicine used to treat and prevent high blood levels of uric acid)
- gemfibrozil (a fibric acid medicine for lowering cholesterol)

Omeprazole is used to treat excess stomach acid in conditions such as stomach ulcers, heartburn or gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), active duodenal ulcer, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and erosive esophagitis.
Omeprazole may also be given together with antibiotics to treat gastric ulcers caused by infection with Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), in adult patients.
Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) that works by blocking the acid pump in your stomach, reducing how much acid it makes and giving irritated or damaged tissue a chance to heal.
Omeprazole brand names are Prilosec, Prilosec OTC, and generic brands are available.

Over-the-counter omeprazole is used for:
- frequent heartburn that occurs 2 or more days a week in adults 18 years and older

Over-the-counter omeprazole is used for:
- frequent heartburn that occurs 2 or more days a week in adults 18 years and older
- It is taken as a 14-day course, once a day for 14 days in a row. It may take 1 to 4 days to reach its full effect, so it is not used for immediate relief of symptoms. Do not take it for longer than 14 days, and do not start another 14-day course within 4 months, unless your doctor tells you to.
Omeprazole can cause kidney problems. Tell your doctor if you are urinating less than usual, or if you have blood in your urine.
Omeprazole is not to be used for the immediate relief of heartburn symptoms.
Omeprazole may cause new or worsening symptoms of lupus. Tell your doctor if you have joint pain and a skin rash on your cheeks or arms that worsens in sunlight.
You may be more likely to have a broken bone while taking this medicine long term or more than once per day.

You should not use omeprazole if you are allergic to it, or if:
- you are also allergic to medicines like omeprazole, such as esomeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, rabeprazole, Nexium, Prevacid, Protonix, and others;
- you had breathing problems, kidney problems, or a severe allergic reaction after taking omeprazole in the past; or
- you also take HIV medication that contains rilpivirine (such as Complera, Edurant, Odefsey, Juluca).
Taking omeprazole long-term may cause you to develop stomach growths called fundic gland polyps. Talk with your doctor about this risk.

If you use this medicine for longer than 3 years, you could develop a vitamin B-12 deficiency. Talk to your doctor if you develop symptoms such as shortness of breath, lightheadedness, irregular heartbeat, muscle weakness, pale skin, feeling tired, mood changes, and tingling or numbness in the arms and legs.

Gabapentin is FDA-approved to treat partial onset seizures in patients 3 years and older (used with other seizure medicines) and nerve pain from shingles (postherpetic neuralgia) in adults. A related product, gabapentin enacarbil (Horizant), is approved for moderate to severe restless legs syndrome in adults.

Doctors also prescribe gabapentin off-label for other types of nerve pain, including diabetic nerve pain (diabetic neuropathy), and for anxiety, fibromyalgia, hot flashes, and alcohol withdrawal. Off-label means that the condition it is being prescribed for is not an FDA-approved indication.

Important: Gralise and Horizant are not substitutes for Neurontin or generic gabapentin, even at the same milligram dose. The release profile differs, and switching without a prescriber's instruction can significantly change blood levels.

Gabapentin works by calming overactive electrical signals in the brain and nervous system. It does this by binding to the alpha-2-delta subunit of calcium channels in nerve cells, which is thought to normalize chemical signals nerves send to each other and results in a calmer, less excitable nerve circuit.

Gabapentin is not an opioid, sedative, or anti-inflammatory painkiller. It works directly on the nerves, which is why it helps nerve-related pain and why it isn't useful for everyday pain like headaches or sprains. Most people need 1 to 2 weeks of regular dosing for the full effect to build up.

Respiratory depression. Gabapentin can cause life-threatening breathing problems (respiratory depression), especially if you already have a breathing disorder (such as COPD), are elderly, or if you use other medicines that can make you drowsy or slow your breathing, such as opioids or CNS depressants. Seek emergency medical attention if you have very slow breathing.

Abrupt or rapid discontinuation. Seizures may occur if you stop using gabapentin suddenly. Ask your doctor before stopping the medicine. Stopping abruptly can cause withdrawal symptoms such as anxiety, trouble sleeping, nausea, pain, and sweating.
The most common side effects of gabapentin are dizziness, drowsiness (somnolence), swelling in the hands or feet (peripheral edema), and tiredness.
You should not take gabapentin if you are allergic to it.

Usual Gabapentin Dose for Epilepsy (immediate-release):
Patients 12 years and older Dose: starting dose gabapentin 300 mg 3 times a day, which may be titrated up to a maximum dose of 600 mg 3 times a day if needed.
- Antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium (such as Maalox) can reduce gabapentin absorption. Take gabapentin at least 2 hours after an antacid.
- Morphine can increase gabapentin levels, which may increase drowsiness and the risk of breathing problems. Your doctor may adjust your dose.

Sertraline is FDA-approved to treat six conditions in adults:
- Major depressive disorder (MDD), the clinical term for depression.
- Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), where unwanted thoughts drive repeated behaviors.
- Panic disorder, which causes sudden attacks of intense fear along with physical symptoms.
- Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), which can follow a frightening or traumatic event.
- Social anxiety disorder (SAD), also called social phobia.
- Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a severe form of premenstrual symptoms.

In children and teenagers, sertraline is approved only for OCD, from age 6 upward. Its safety and effectiveness have not been established in children under 6 years of age, or in children and teenagers for any condition other than OCD.

Sertraline belongs to a group of medicines called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. It increases serotonin activity in the brain by blocking the reuptake of serotonin (a chemical messenger that nerve cells use to communicate) back into nerve cells, so more of it stays available. Sertraline has only very weak effects on the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine, and it does not block monoamine oxidase.
Sertraline is available as tablets (25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg), oral solution (20 mg/mL), and capsules (150 mg and 200 mg).

Sertraline carries a boxed warning, the FDA's most serious type of warning. Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, teenagers, and young adults in short-term studies.

Do not take sertraline with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI), or within 14 days of stopping one, because of the risk of serotonin syndrome. This includes the antibiotic linezolid and intravenous methylene blue. You also need to wait at least 14 days after stopping sertraline before starting an MAOI.
Do not take sertraline with pimozide, an antipsychotic medicine. Do not take sertraline oral solution if you take disulfiram (Antabuse), because the solution contains alcohol.
Sertraline can raise the risk of bleeding, particularly if you also take aspirin, NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen, other antiplatelet medicines, warfarin, or other anticoagulants.
Sertraline oral solution contains 12% alcohol and is not recommended during pregnancy, because there is no known safe level of alcohol exposure in pregnancy.

Low levels of sertraline and its breakdown products pass into breast milk. In a pooled analysis of 53 mother and infant pairs, exclusively breastfed infants had an average of 2% of the sertraline levels measured in their mothers' blood, ranging from 0% to 15%. No side effects were seen in those infants. There is no information on whether sertraline affects milk production. Talk with your doctor about the benefits of breastfeeding alongside your need for treatment.

Escitalopram is an antidepressant belonging to a group of drugs called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). It affects chemicals in the brain that may be unbalanced in people with depression or anxiety.
Escitalopram is used to treat major depressive disorder in adults and adolescents at least 12 years old.
Escitalopram is also used to treat anxiety in adults and children at least 7 years old.
You should not use escitalopram you also take pimozide or citalopram (Celexa).

Do not use escitalopram within 14 days before or 14 days after you have used an MAO inhibitor, such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, or tranylcypromine.

You should not use this medicine if you are allergic to escitalopram or citalopram (Celexa), or if:
- you also take pimozide.
Escitalopram is not approved for use by anyone younger than 7 years old.

Using escitalopram with other drugs that make you drowsy can worsen this effect. Ask your doctor before using opioid medication, a sleeping pill, a muscle relaxer, or medicine for anxiety or seizures.
Tell your doctor about all your current medicines, especially a blood thinner such as warfarin, Coumadin, or Jantoven.

Semaglutide works by reducing appetite, delaying gastric emptying, increasing insulin release, and lowering the amount of glucagon released. Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist that mimics the behavior of the GLP-1 hormone, which is naturally released after eating.

Ozempic tablets and injections are FDA-approved in adults for:
- type 2 diabetes to improve blood sugar control
- reducing the risk of a major cardiovascular event (such as heart attack, stroke, or death) in type 2 diabetic patients who are at high risk for these events

Ozempic injection is also FDA-approved in adults for:
- reducing the risk of kidney function decline, kidney failure, and cardiovascular death in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (CKD)

Wegovy tablets and injections are FDA-approved in adults for:
- weight loss and weight management in adults with obesity or adults who are overweight and have a weight-related medical problem (e.g., blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, or high cholesterol)

Wegovy injection is also FDA-approved for:
- weight loss and weight management patients with obesity who are 12 years and older

Wegovy injection is also FDA-approved for:
- weight loss and weight management patients with obesity who are 12 years and older
- non-cirrhotic metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) in adults with moderate to advanced liver fibrosis (consistent with stages F2 to F3 fibrosis), this is an accelerated approval.

Rybelsus oral tablets are FDA-approved in adults for:
- type 2 diabetes in adults to help control blood sugar levels.
- reducing the risk of major cardiovascular events (such as heart attack, stroke, or death) in type 2 diabetic patients with known heart disease.

Semaglutide has a boxed warning for the risk of thyroid C-cell tumors. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA. Semaglutide may cause serious side effects, including possible thyroid tumors and thyroid cancer.
You should not use semaglutide if you have multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (tumors in your glands) or a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer.
In animal studies, semaglutide caused thyroid tumors or thyroid cancer. It is not known whether these effects would occur in people. Ask your doctor about your risk.

Men and women should stop using semaglutide at least 2 months before they plan to get pregnant. Ask your doctor for a safer medicine to use during this time. Controlling diabetes is very important during pregnancy, as is gaining the right amount of weight. Even if you are overweight, losing weight during pregnancy could harm the unborn baby.

- Start Ozempic with a 0.25 mg subcutaneous injection (injection under the skin) once weekly for 4 weeks. The 0.25 mg dosage is intended for treatment initiation and is not effective for glycemic control.

Semaglutide can slow your digestion, and it may take longer for your body to absorb any medicines you take by mouth.

Adderall (mixed amphetamine and dextroamphetamine salts) is a central nervous system stimulant used to treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and a sleep disorder called narcolepsy. Adderall contains a combination of amphetamine and dextroamphetamine, which affect chemicals in the brain and nerves that contribute to hyperactivity and impulse control.
- For ADHD, Adderall is used in children 3 to 17 years of age and in adults. It may help increase attention and decrease impulsiveness and hyperactivity.
- For narcolepsy, Adderall is used in people 6 years and older.

Adderall is a federally controlled substance (CII) because it contains amphetamine, which can be a target for people who abuse prescription medicines or street drugs. Keep Adderall in a safe place to protect it from theft. Never give your Adderall to anyone else, because it may cause death or harm them. Selling or giving away Adderall is against the law.
Adderall (mixed amphetamine and dextroamphetamine salts) was FDA-approved on January 19, 1960. Extended-release formulations of Adderall (Adderall XR) are only used to treat ADHD.
Adderall has a Boxed Warning for abuse, misuse, and addiction.

Adderall may lead to physical dependence after prolonged use, even if taken as directed. Your healthcare provider should check you or your child for the risk of abuse, misuse, and addiction before starting treatment and will monitor you or your child during treatment. Tell your healthcare provider if you or your child has ever abused or been dependent on alcohol, prescription medicines, or street drugs.

Do not use Adderall if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days, such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, or tranylcypromine, or if you have received a methylene blue injection. A dangerous drug interaction could occur.

Do not take Adderall if you or your child:
- are allergic to amphetamine products or any of the ingredients in Adderall (see ingredients below)
- are taking, or have taken within the past 14 days, an MAO inhibitor, including the antibiotic linezolid or the intravenous medicine methylene blue.
- have a rare adrenal gland tumor called pheochromocytoma.

Taking Adderall during pregnancy can cause premature birth, low birth weight, or withdrawal symptoms in the newborn baby. Tell your healthcare provider if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. There is a pregnancy registry that collects information about the health of females exposed to Adderall and their babies.

Adderall passes into breast milk and may harm a nursing baby. You should not breastfeed during treatment with Adderall. Talk to your healthcare provider about the best way to feed the baby during treatment.

Usual adult dose for ADHD:
Immediate-release (IR):
- Initial dose: 5 mg orally 1 or 2 times a day.

Extended-release (XR), for patients starting treatment for the first time or switching from another medication:
- Initial dose: 20 mg orally once a day.

Usual adult dose for narcolepsy:
Immediate-release (IR):
- Initial dose: 10 mg orally per day in divided doses.
