Potassium chloride is used to prevent or to treat low blood levels of potassium (hypokalemia).
You should not use potassium chloride if you have high levels of potassium in your blood (hyperkalemia), or if you also take a "potassium-sparing" diuretic.

To be sure potassium chloride is helping your condition, your blood may need to be tested often. Your heart rate may also be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG (sometimes called an EKG) to measure electrical activity of the heart. This test will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium. Do not miss any scheduled appointments.

Do not crush, chew, or suck on an extended-release tablet or capsule. Swallow the pill whole unless your doctor or pharmacist tells you your specific tablet can be broken. Crushing or chewing the pill may cause too much of the drug to be released at one time. Sucking on a tablet can irritate your mouth or throat. Take potassium chloride with food or just after a meal.
You should not use potassium chloride if you are allergic to it, or if:
- you take a "potassium-sparing" diuretic (water pill) such as amiloride, spironolactone, or triamterene.
Take potassium chloride with a full glass of water. Take potassium chloride with food or just after a meal.

Mix the powder form of this medicine with at least 4 ounces (one-half cup) of cold water or fruit juice before taking. Drink the mixture slowly, over 5 to 10 minutes in all. To make sure you get the entire dose, add a little more water to the same glass, swirl gently and drink right away.

Avoid taking supplements or using other products that contain potassium without first asking your doctor. Salt substitutes or low-salt dietary products often contain potassium. If you take certain products together you may accidentally get too much potassium. Read the label of any other medicine you are using to see if it contains potassium.

Common potassium chloride side effects may include:
- nausea, vomiting, diarrhea;
- gas, stomach pain; or
- the appearance of a potassium chloride tablet in your stool.

Tell your doctor about all your current medicines and any you start or stop using, especially:
- a diuretic or "water pill"; or
- heart or blood pressure medication.
- NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) such as aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, celecoxib, diclofenac, indomethacin, or meloxicam.
Hydroxyzine is a prescription antihistamine used to treat anxiety and tension, itching from allergic skin conditions, and sedation before and after general anesthesia.

- Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) tablets in 10 mg, 25 mg, and 50 mg strengths
- Hydroxyzine hydrochloride oral solution (a syrup) containing 10 mg in each 5 mL
- Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules in 25 mg
There is also a hydroxyzine hydrochloride injection. It is given into a muscle by a healthcare professional and is never given into a vein or under the skin.
The injection is also approved for nausea and vomiting and is usually given in hospital or clinic settings. It should not be used for nausea and vomiting caused by pregnancy.

Hydroxyzine has not been studied for long-term use in anxiety. Studies have not assessed whether it still works as an anti-anxiety medicine beyond four months. Your doctor should review from time to time whether you still need it.

The two salts also had different brand names. Vistaril was the brand name for hydroxyzine pamoate, and Atarax was the brand name for hydroxyzine hydrochloride. Both brands have been discontinued in the United States, and hydroxyzine is now available as a generic medicine.
Hydroxyzine also blocks histamine, a chemical your body releases during an allergic reaction. This is what relieves itching.

Laboratory and clinical studies have also shown that hydroxyzine relaxes skeletal muscle, widens the airways (bronchodilation), and reduces pain. These are effects that have been observed rather than uses the medicine is approved for.

Dosage for anxiety and tension:
- Adults: 50 to 100 mg four times a day

Dosage for itching:
- Adults: 25 mg three or four times a day

Dosage for sedation before and after surgery:
- Adults: 50 to 100 mg
- Children: 0.6 mg for each kilogram of body weight
The most common side effects of hydroxyzine are drowsiness, dry mouth, and headache. These are usually mild and do not last long.

In rare cases, hydroxyzine can cause a serious skin reaction called acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). Signs include fever together with many small, shallow, pus-filled spots appearing across large areas of swollen, red skin. If you have had AGEP or another allergic reaction to hydroxyzine, you should also avoid cetirizine and levocetirizine, because a similar reaction can happen with those medicines.
Hydroxyzine has also been linked to a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, which can lead to a serious irregular heartbeat known as Torsade de Pointes.

If you are given hydroxyzine by injection, tell your healthcare provider straight away about severe pain, swelling, or skin changes where the injection was given. In rare cases, the injection has caused serious damage to the surrounding tissue, including tissue death (necrosis) and gangrene, which has needed surgery to treat.

Do not take hydroxyzine if you:
- are allergic to hydroxyzine or to any ingredient in the medicine
- are allergic to cetirizine or levocetirizine
- have a prolonged QT interval, a heart rhythm finding seen on an electrocardiogram (ECG)
- are in early pregnancy
Hydroxyzine should not be given to women who are breastfeeding. It is not known whether hydroxyzine passes into breast milk, but many medicines do.
The oral solution contains a small amount of alcohol, 0.5% by volume, and is sweetened with sucrose. Tell your doctor if either of these matters for you.
No. Alcohol's effects may be stronger while you are taking hydroxyzine. You should also avoid other medicines that slow down the central nervous system.
No. Hydroxyzine is not a controlled substance and has no DEA schedule. This applies to both hydroxyzine hydrochloride and hydroxyzine pamoate.

Hydroxyzine makes the effects of central nervous system depressants stronger. If you take hydroxyzine with any of the following, your doctor may need to lower the dose of the other medicine:
- narcotic (opioid) pain medicines
- non-narcotic pain medicines
- barbiturates
Hydroxyzine may increase the effects of meperidine and barbiturates when used before anesthesia, so your doctor will adjust these doses for you individually.

Care is needed if you take other medicines that can affect heart rhythm by prolonging the QT interval. These include:
- heart rhythm medicines such as quinidine, procainamide, amiodarone, and sotalol
- certain antipsychotics such as ziprasidone, iloperidone, clozapine, quetiapine, and chlorpromazine
- certain antidepressants such as citalopram and fluoxetine
- certain antibiotics such as azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin, gatifloxacin, and moxifloxacin
- other medicines such as pentamidine, methadone, ondansetron, and droperidol

Allopurinol belongs to a class of medications called xanthine oxidase inhibitors. It works by reducing the production of uric acid in the body. High levels of uric acid may cause gout attacks or kidney stones.

Allopurinol is used to treat gout (a type of arthritis in which uric acid, a naturally occurring substance in the body, builds up in the joints and causes sudden attacks of redness, swelling, pain, and heat in one or more joints). Allopurinol is used to prevent gout attacks, not to treat them once they occur. Allopurinol does not need to be stopped during an acute flare.

Allopurinol is also used to treat high levels of uric acid that builds up in the blood as tumors break down in people with certain types of cancer who are being treated with chemotherapy medications. It is also used to treat kidney stones that have come back in people who have high levels of uric acid in their urine.

Cetirizine is a second generation antihistamine that reduces the natural chemical histamine in the body. Histamine can produce symptoms of sneezing, itching, watery eyes, and runny nose.
Cetirizine is used to treat cold or allergy symptoms such as sneezing, itching, watery eyes, or runny nose.

Cetirizine is also used to treat an allergic reaction, itching and swelling caused by chronic urticaria (hives) and minimizes or eliminates the symptoms of perennial allergic rhinitis, seasonal allergic rhinitis, chronic idiopathic urticaria, allergic asthma, physical urticaria, and atopic dermatitis.

Tell your doctor if you regularly use other medicines that make you sleepy (such as other cold or allergy medicine, narcotic pain medicine, sleeping pills, muscle relaxers, and medicine for seizures, depression, or anxiety). They can add to sleepiness caused by cetirizine.

If you are taking cetirizine for hives, get emergency medical help immediately if you have trouble swallowing, dizziness, swelling of the tongue or around the mouth, trouble speaking, drooling, or wheezing. Cetirizine is not a substitute for an epinephrine injector. Do not use cetirizine to prevent hives from known causes such as foods, insect stings, or medicines. Call your doctor if your hives do not improve after 3 days, if they last more than 6 weeks, or if they are an unusual color, look bruised or blistered, or do not itch.

Rarely, some people have reported severe itching when stopping cetirizine after daily, long-term use of at least a few months or several years. If you experience widespread, severe itching on stopping this medication, contact your healthcare provider.
You should not use this medication if you are allergic to cetirizine, levocetirizine, hydroxyzine, or any of the ingredients in the product.
Ask a health professional before using this medicine if you are pregnant. Cetirizine is not recommended if you are breast-feeding.
Cetirizine is indicated for chronic idiopathic urticaria in adults and children 6 months of age and older.
You may take cetirizine with or without food.
Avoid drinking alcohol. It can increase some of the side effects of cetirizine.

Q: Can you take Benadryl and cetirizine together? A: Benadryl should not be taken at the same time as cetirizine because it can increase side effects such as dizziness, drowsiness, and difficulty concentrating. Some people, especially the elderly or children, may also find their thinking, judgement, and coordination impaired. You should also not drink alcohol while taking either of these medications because it can make these side effects worse.

Q: Can cetirizine raise blood pressure? A: Cetirizine does not increase blood pressure and blood pressure is not listed as a side effect in the product information. But cetirizine can be found in combination with other medications, such as pseudoephedrine in products such as Zyrtec-D, and pseudoephedrine does increase blood pressure.

Q: How long does it take for cetirizine to work? A: Cetirizine is an allergy medicine that usually starts to work within about 20 to 60 minutes after you take it. Many people notice less sneezing and itching within the first hour, especially if they take it on an empty stomach. One dose of cetirizine generally provides relief for up to 24 hours, so most people only need to take it once a day.

Cyclobenzaprine is a prescription muscle relaxant used short-term to relieve muscle spasms caused by sprains, strains, and injuries, including low back and neck pain. It is used together with rest and physical therapy to help relieve the pain, tenderness, and limited movement caused by muscle spasm. 1,2

Cyclobenzaprine is also used to treat fibromyalgia in adults, where it can help reduce pain. For fibromyalgia, it is taken as a sublingual (under the tongue) tablet at bedtime under the brand name Tonmya. In clinical trials, Tonmya significantly reduced fibromyalgia pain compared with placebo over 14 weeks, and close to half of treated patients achieved at least a 30% improvement in pain. 3
The Flexeril brand has been discontinued, but cyclobenzaprine is available as generic tablets and as the brand-name products Amrix (extended-release capsules) and Fexmid. 2,4

Cyclobenzaprine works by reducing the nerve signals in the brain that drive muscle tone and spasm, which allows tight, overactive muscles to relax. It acts within the central nervous system, primarily at the level of the brain stem, and does not act on the muscles themselves or at the junction between nerves and muscle. 1,2 Because cyclobenzaprine works through the nervous system in this way, it will not relieve muscle spasm caused by central nervous system disease, such as cerebral palsy or spinal cord disease. 1,2
The way cyclobenzaprine works in fibromyalgia is not known. Laboratory studies show it blocks several receptor types, including serotonin (5-HT2A), histamine, and muscarinic receptors. 3

Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic (water pill) used for heart failure, high blood pressure, fluid build-up (edema) caused by liver or kidney disease, and a hormone condition called primary hyperaldosteronism. Spironolactone is sometimes prescribed off-label for women with acne or excessive facial hair growth (hirsutism).

Spironolactone works by blocking a hormone called aldosterone, which causes your body to pass more salt and water in your urine while keeping potassium in. This is why it is called potassium-sparing, and it is what makes spironolactone different from most other water pills, which flush potassium out.
Spironolactone also blocks androgens such as testosterone from binding to the androgen receptor, which explains several of its side effects, including breast tenderness and breast growth.

Spironolactone is FDA-approved to treat adults with:
- Heart failure (NYHA Class III-IV) with a reduced ejection fraction to help live longer, reduce swelling, and reduce the need for hospital stays. It is taken alongside other heart failure medicines rather than on its own.

Reported spironolactone side effects include breast and nipple pain in both men and women, a lower sex drive, trouble getting or keeping an erection, irregular or missed periods, bleeding after menopause, dizziness, headache, drowsiness, feeling sluggish, leg cramps, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach cramps, indigestion, hair thinning, and itching.

The most common side effect of spironolactone is breast growth in men, known as gynecomastia. In the main heart failure study, about 9 in 100 men taking an average of 26 mg a day developed it. The chance goes up on higher doses. It can start anywhere from one or two months into treatment to more than a year later, and it usually goes away after the medicine is stopped.

Do not take spironolactone if you have a high potassium level in your blood, if you have Addison's disease (an adrenal gland disorder), or if you are taking eplerenone (Inspra), another medicine of the same type.

Spironolactone can raise your potassium to a dangerous level. A high potassium level can cause a life-threatening change in your heart rhythm, and it often causes no symptoms until it is already high. Your doctor should check your potassium with a blood test within a week of you starting spironolactone or having your dose changed, and regularly after that.

Your risk of high potassium is greater if your kidneys do not work well, if you take potassium supplements or a salt substitute containing potassium, or if you take an ACE inhibitor, an ARB, an NSAID, heparin, or trimethoprim.
Do not use potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium unless your doctor has specifically told you to.
Spironolactone should be avoided in pregnancy where possible, because it blocks male hormones and may affect how a male baby develops.

Spironolactone dosage for heart failure:
Treatment starts at spironolactone 25 mg once a day, provided your potassium level is 5.0 mEq/L or lower and your kidney function (eGFR) is above 50. If you tolerate that, the dose may go up to 50 mg once a day. If your potassium rises too high, the dose may drop to 25 mg every other day. If your eGFR is between 30 and 50, your doctor may start you at 25 mg every other day because of the higher risk of high potassium.

Spironolactone dosage for high blood pressure:
The usual starting dose is spironolactone 25 mg to 100 mg a day, taken as one dose or split into two. The dose can be adjusted every two weeks. Doses above 100 mg a day do not generally lower blood pressure any further.

Spironolactone dosage for fluid build-up (edema):
The usual starting dose is 100 mg a day, taken as one dose or split into two, and the dose can range from 25 mg to 200 mg a day. If you have cirrhosis, treatment is started in hospital and increased slowly. When spironolactone is the only water pill being used, it is given for at least five days before the dose is increased.
